children.text: I'll check what mods can do in the desktop app, and what's public about how the Mac app is built.
Short answer: it isn't easier. The hard part stays the same, and getting code into the app is harder.

children: Mods don't reach the chat you use.
Mods run only in Claude Code in the terminal and in the Code tab of the desktop app, not in regular chats
. That matches the spec's mod spike notes. A mod might see raw markdown there, but only for Code-tab sessions, not the chats where you're running the trial.

children.text: **The only other way in is unofficial.** The Mac app is an Electron app, and Electron bundles a version of Chromium. People have injected code into it by launching it with --remote-debugging-port=9222, then calling Runtime.evaluate() to inject a <style> tag into the live DOM. There's also an installer that generates a modified version of the Claude Desktop client with extension support enabled. Both are third-party hacks:

- They break when the app updates. One such tool already warns that the CSS selectors for message elements and the stop button may not match the current Claude Desktop UI.
- An open debugging port lets any local process control your signed-in app.
- You'd have to launch the app in a special way every time.

children: The hard part doesn't go away.
The desktop chat is the same claude.ai interface running inside Electron
, so the renderer would still get page HTML with labels split across elements, just as in Chrome. The copy-button testing approach works the same in both, so the choice doesn't affect how you'd test.
What does matter is where you read replies.
A Chrome extension only styles claude.ai in Chrome.
Do you read most of these replies in the Mac app or in Chrome?
If it's the Mac app, the extension won't show up where you look, and that's the real cost of going web-first. If it's Chrome, the spec's plan stands.
